h1: The 7 Best Docking Stations for Chromebooks of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Chromebook Docking Stations: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: seven docks for Chromebooks, from certified dual-4K units to triple-monitor hubs, compared on display limits and charging.
summary: The Plugable 12-in-1 is the best docking station for Chromebooks, certified for ChromeOS with dual 4K through DisplayLink and built-in Ethernet. The Plugable UD-MSTH2 offers dual 4K at 60Hz driverless, and the Plugable Triple Display drives three screens on capable Chromebooks. The Anker 8-in-1 is the budget hub, and the Selore, the 14-in-1 hub and the Anker Prime serve niche needs.
intro: Chromebooks are why so many generic docks disappoint. Many models drive only one external display through a plain USB-C port, so a hub that promises two monitors can quietly give you one. The dock that works is the one that either sidesteps that limit with DisplayLink software or states ChromeOS support outright, and the box rarely tells you which.

Our editors weighed seven docks by their listings, scoring them on the Primea framework with ChromeOS support, video method, charging wattage, refresh limits and Thunderbolt needs carrying the most weight. Prices are buckets. Check your Chromebook's spec sheet for external display support before spending, because a dock cannot add outputs the laptop lacks, and the docks here cannot change that, so a wrong guess costs you a return.

products.name: Plugable 12-in-1 Dual 4K USB-C Docking Station (Chromebook Certified)
products.verdict: Chromebook certified, with dual 4K via DisplayLink.
products.description:
The Plugable 12-in-1 is certified for Chromebook, Windows and ChromeOS, and gives dual 4K display via DisplayLink. It charges at 60W and has Ethernet in a 12-in-1 layout, in the $100 to $200 bucket. DisplayLink compresses video through a driver, which lets a Chromebook with a single video output drive two screens.

It ranks first because the Chromebook certification removes the main uncertainty, and the DisplayLink route works where plain USB-C docks fail. The UD-MSTH2 matches dual 4K at 60Hz but without certification.

Buy it for Chromebook owners who need dual external monitors. The caveats are the 60W charging ceiling and a price above generic hubs. Skip it if one external display is enough.
products.idealFor: Chromebook owners who need dual external monitors.

products.name: Plugable USB-C Docking Station Dual Monitor 4K 60Hz (UD-MSTH2)
products.verdict: Dual 4K 60Hz via two HDMI ports, driverless on ChromeOS.
products.description:
The UD-MSTH2 offers dual 4K 60Hz over two HDMI ports, 65W charging, gigabit Ethernet and USB-C plus three USB-A 5Gbps ports. It is driverless on Windows and ChromeOS, in the $100 to $200 bucket. Driverless means plugging in and working, with no software to install.

It ranks second because it lacks the Chromebook certification, though 65W is five watts more than the 12-in-1. It depends on your Chromebook's port supporting multi-monitor output, which the certified dock bypasses.

Buy it for dual 4K desks that do not need the certification premium. The caveats are the lack of certification and the need for a capable USB-C port. Skip it if you want a certified dock.

products.name: Plugable USB-C Triple Display Docking Station
products.verdict: Three HDMI outputs and 100W charging for newer Chromebooks.
products.description:
The Plugable Triple Display dock has three HDMI outputs, one at 4K 30Hz and two at 1080p 60Hz. It provides 100W USB-C Power Delivery and six USB 5Gbps ports, and works with Windows, macOS and ChromeOS, in the $100 to $200 bucket. 100W is generous for a Chromebook, leaving headroom for a second device.

It ranks third because three screens only work if the Chromebook supports it, and 4K is limited to 30Hz, which feels laggy for desktop work. It beats the Selore on stated support for ChromeOS.

Buy it if you own a newer Thunderbolt Chromebook and want three screens. The caveats are 4K at 30Hz and a need for a capable host. Skip it if you need 4K at 60Hz.
products.idealFor: Newer Thunderbolt Chromebook owners wanting three screens.

products.name: Anker Laptop Docking Station Dual Monitor, 8-in-1 USB C Hub
products.verdict: An 8-in-1 hub with 85W PD for under $100.
products.description:
The Anker 8-in-1 lists dual monitor output through two HDMI ports, 85W Power Delivery, 1 Gbps Ethernet and an SD card reader, in the $50 to $100 bucket. 85W covers any Chromebook charger rating and leaves room for a phone.

It ranks fourth because it makes no Chromebook claims, so its dual-monitor output may drop to one screen on many models. A dock that lists two HDMI ports on a Chromebook that only supports one display will mirror, not extend.

Buy it as a budget hub for ports and one extra screen. The caveats are no Chromebook claim and dual output not guaranteed. Skip it if you need two monitors on ChromeOS.
products.idealFor: Budget buyers who need ports and one extra screen.
products.skipIf: You need two monitors on ChromeOS.

products.name: Selore Laptop Docking Station 3 Monitors, Triple 4K Display
products.verdict: Triple 4K display with 100W PD at a budget price.
products.description:
The Selore dock is listed for triple 4K display, with three HDMI and two DisplayPort outputs, 100W Power Delivery, 10Gbps USB A and C and gigabit Ethernet. It adds an SD and microSD reader and smart display, in the $50 to $100 bucket. The 10Gbps ports are fast enough for an external SSD.

It ranks fifth because it makes no ChromeOS claim, and triple 4K is only possible on a Chromebook whose graphics and port can drive it. Against the Plugable Triple Display, it lists higher resolution but less certainty.

Buy it for Thunderbolt Chromebooks or mixed-device desks. The caveats are no Chromebook claim and a need for a capable host. Skip it if you want certified ChromeOS support.

products.name: USB C Laptop Docking Station Dual Monitor HDMI, 14-in-1 USB C Hub
products.verdict: A 14-in-1 hub packed with ports at the lowest price.
products.description:
This 14-in-1 hub offers dual HDMI plus DisplayPort output, 100W PD pass-through, four USB-A ports, two USB-C ports, SD and TF readers and audio, in the $25 to $50 bucket. It packs the most ports at the lowest price.

It ranks sixth because it states nothing about ChromeOS, so you must know your Chromebook's display limits before relying on it. A port count does not help if the host cannot drive the screens.

Buy it if you know your Chromebook's display limits and want lots of ports for little money. The caveats are no ChromeOS claim and display limits you must check. Skip it if you want certified compatibility.
cons: Display limits are yours to check
products.idealFor: Buyers who know their Chromebook's display limits.

products.name: Anker Prime Docking Station, 14-Port with 160W Max Output
products.verdict: A 160W dock that shares a Chromebook with a power-hungry laptop.
products.description:
The Anker Prime is a 14-port dock with 160W max output, 10Gbps data transfer, dual 4K displays and a Real-Time Smart Interface display. It sits in the $100 to $200 bucket. 160W is far above what a Chromebook draws, but it suits a shared desk with a workstation laptop.

It ranks last because it is overbuilt for a Chromebook alone, though it suits households sharing a dock with a higher-power machine. It has no ChromeOS claim, so display support is yours to confirm.

Buy it for homes where a Chromebook shares the dock with a power-hungry laptop. The caveats are the excess power and no ChromeOS claim. Skip it if you only own a Chromebook.
cons: More power than a Chromebook needs
products.idealFor: Households sharing a dock with a higher-power laptop.

whatMatters.detail: Many Chromebooks drive only one external display over USB-C. A certified or DisplayLink dock avoids that limit. Look for Chromebook certified or ChromeOS on the listing, and treat a dock that says nothing about ChromeOS as a gamble if you need two screens. The listing's silence usually means a one-screen limit on ChromeOS.

DisplayLink sends video over USB using a driver, and MST splits one video signal into several. DisplayLink works on more hosts. Check the listing for which one the dock uses, because an MST dock still depends on the Chromebook supporting multiple streams over its port. DisplayLink avoids that dependence at the cost of a driver.

Docks charge through the same cable. Chromebooks often need 45W to 65W. Match the dock's PD to your charger rating, and avoid docks that cap below it, since the laptop will charge slowly or drain while you work. The 12-in-1 lists 60W and the UD-MSTH2 65W. A larger rating is harmless, because the laptop draws only what it needs.

Triple-display docks may cap one screen at 4K 30Hz. That feels laggy for desktop use. Read the per-port refresh rate, such as the Plugable Triple Display's single 4K 30Hz output, and check that your main screen gets the full rate. Put the 30Hz screen to the side for reference windows.

Newer Chromebooks with Thunderbolt can drive more screens. Older ones cannot. Check your Chromebook's spec sheet before choosing a triple dock, and look for external display support by name, because the port label alone does not tell you what the laptop can output. The manual or the maker's support page lists the limits.

faq.q: Can a Chromebook run two external monitors?
faq.a: Some can through DisplayLink docks like the Plugable 12-in-1. Many only support one over plain USB-C, so check the dock's ChromeOS line and confirm your model's external display support. A dock cannot add outputs that the laptop lacks.

faq.q: What mistake do buyers make with Chromebook docks?
faq.a: They buy a generic hub and expect two screens. Check the ChromeOS line first, because the Anker 8-in-1 and 14-in-1 hubs make no ChromeOS claim, so the second screen may mirror or never light up. Read the compatibility line first.

faq.q: Is the certified dock worth it over the UD-MSTH2?
faq.a: If you want certainty, yes. The UD-MSTH2 offers 65W and dual 4K 60Hz without certification, so it suits buyers who know their Chromebook supports it. The certified dock costs a little more for peace of mind.

faq.q: Do I need a driver on ChromeOS?
faq.a: The UD-MSTH2 is driverless on ChromeOS. The 12-in-1 uses DisplayLink, which is listed as certified, so setup is still simple. Both plug in and work within a minute on a supported Chromebook.

faq.q: How do I check my Chromebook's display limits?
faq.a: Look at the spec sheet for its USB-C display support. Match it to the dock, and search for the maker's list of supported displays. Chromebook makers publish the number of monitors each model can drive.

faq.q: Can I use a triple display dock on any Chromebook?
faq.a: No. The Plugable Triple Display and Selore need a capable, often Thunderbolt, Chromebook. Check yours before ordering a three-screen dock, since the extra output will sit unused on a laptop that drives only one screen.

finalTake: Buy the certified Plugable 12-in-1 if you need two external monitors and want certainty. The UD-MSTH2 is a cheaper way to dual 4K without the certification. Choose the Triple Display or Selore only with a capable Thunderbolt Chromebook. The Anker 8-in-1 and 14-in-1 hubs are for buyers who already know their Chromebook's display limits.
